section.name: Introduction
section.t: The IPREF UDP Tunnel Protocol is used to encapsulate packets to be exchanged by IPREF gateways. It can also be used in the IPREF Introspection Protocol by IPREF gateways to send packets containing IPREF addresses to hosts on the local network.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: IPREF Terminology
section.t: IPREF - short name referring to technology described in this document, pronounced I-P-REF
context address - a native address component of an IPREF address
reference - an unsigned integer component of an IPREF address
IPREF address - addressing unit used with IPREF, a combination of a context address and a reference
encoding network - network representing IPREF addresses in native form
IPREF gateway - a device, or software component, that performs IPREF address rewriting

section.name: IPREF UDP Tunnel Protocol (IUTP)
section.t: IPREF, , does not specifically require a tunnel. The references can be added to the packets using standard extension mechanisms designed for the relevant network protocols. Unfortunately in case of IPv4 and IPv6, these mechanisms prove unreliable. In many cases, packets carrying IPv4 options or IPv6 extension headers are placed on the slow path or worse yet are outright dropped. These are serious protocol deficiencies found with both IPv4 and IPv6 which require employing alternative means of transferring reference information with the packets.

One such common mechanism is tunneling via UDP. While there are many UDP tunnels in existence, none fits the needs of IPREF. IPREF references are not meant to be tunneled, rather, IPREF references are meant to be appended to the existing packets. Thus, IUTP is not a classic tunnel. Its main purpose is to attach reference information to existing packet in the payload, rather than in the header, in order to work around deficient protocols which may drop them accidentally while in transit.

section.name: Packet Structure
section.t: A tunnel packet encapsulates a transport layer packet in a UDP packet (with destination port 1045) which also contains a Tunnel Information header, an optional Fragment Information header, and source and destination IPREF addresses.

When an IPREF gateway encapsulates a packet, the original IPv4/IPv6 header is converted into a Tunnel Information (and possibly also Fragment Information) header and the source and destination IPv4/IPv6 addresses are used to determine the Source Reference and Destination Reference fields as well as the destination IPREF gateway. The transport layer header and data are modified as necessary (see "Transport Layer Encapsulation").

The contexts of the source and destination IPREF addresses MAY be omitted (CP=0 in Tunnel Information), in which case the packet is interpreted the same as if both source and destination contexts were set to the Unspecified Context. When a gateway receives a packet which contains the context fields (CP=1), the gateway MUST check that the source and destination contexts match the expected values and drop the packet if they do not.
The outer IPv4/IPv6 packet MUST NOT be fragmented; and, in the case of IPv4, the Don't Fragment bit must be set.
Unless specified otherwise, all fields are in network byte order (big-endian).

figure.name: Packet Structure
figure.artwork: ┌───────────────────────┐ │ IPv4/IPv6 Header │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ UDP Header │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Tunnel Information │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Fragment Information │ (if IF=1 in Tunnel Information) ├───────────────────────┤ │ Source Context │ (if CP=1 in Tunnel Information) ├───────────────────────┤ │ Destination Context │ (if CP=1 in Tunnel Information) ├───────────────────────┤ │ Source Reference │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Destination Reference │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Transport Header │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Payload │ └───────────────────────┘

section.name: Tunnel Information Header
section.t: The tunnel information header is present in every packet and specifies which following headers and fields are present as well as the length of the source and destination reference fields.

When converting from an IPv4 or IPv6 packet, the TTL field is copied unmodified into the tunnel packet. For IPv4 packets, the Don't Fragment bit is also copied. For IPv6 packets, the Don't Fragment bit is always set. The Is Fragment bit is set as necessary. The Protocol field is set as described in "Transport Layer Encapsulation".
The REFL field indicates the length of the Source Reference and Destination Reference fields. These fields SHOULD be as small as their contained references permit.
RES1 : 3 bits - Write zero, drop if non-zero
CP : 1 bit - Contexts Present
REFL : 2 bits - Specifies the length of the references in the header:
IF : 1 bit - Is Fragment
DF : 1 bit - Don't Fragment
RES2 : 8 bits - Write zero, read ignored
TTL : 8 bits - Time to Live
PROTO : 8 bits - Protocol

section.name: Fragment Information Header
section.t: This header is only present if Is Fragment is set. The Fragment Offset, More Fragments, and Identification fields are copied from the corresponding fields in the IPv4 or IPv6 header.
When converting from an IPv4 packet, the high 16 bits of the Identification field are zeroed. When converting to an IPv4 packet, the high 16 bits of the Identification field are discarded.
RES3 : 16 bits - Reserved; must be zero
Fragment Offset : 13 bits - In 8-byte units
RES4 : 2 bits - Reserved; must be zero
MF : 1 bit - More Fragments
Identification : 32 bits

section.name: Source and Destination Context
section.t: The contexts consist of a 1-byte context type followed by the variable-length context value. The length of the context value is determined by the type.
Type : 8 bits
Other values are reserved for future use.

section.name: Unspecified Context (Type = 0)
section.t: This context type indicates that the context should be inferred from the source and destination addresses and ports of the outer IPv4/IPv6 and UDP headers.
Type : 8 bits - 0
Pad : 24 bits - Write zero, drop if non-zero

section.name: IPREF UDP Tunnel over IPv4 Context (Type = 4)
section.t: Type : 8 bits - 4
Pad : 8 bits - Write zero, drop if non-zero
Port : 16 bits - The UDP port of the IPREF tunnel
IPv4 Address : 32 bits - The IPv4 address of the IPREF tunnel

section.name: IPREF UDP Tunnel over IPv6 Context (Type = 6)
section.t: Type : 8 bits - 6
Pad : 8 bits - Write zero, drop if non-zero
Port : 16 bits - The UDP port of the IPREF tunnel
IPv6 Address : 128 bits - The IPv6 address of the IPREF tunnel

section.name: Source and Destination Reference
section.t: Source and destination references are 16-octet long items possibly compressed to 4 or 8 octets as described in . The value of the REFL field in indicates which format is used.

section.name: Transport Layer Encapsulation
section.t: When the transport layer packet is encapsulated or de-encapsulated, some adjustments are made depending on the protocol.
The transport layer protocol is indicated by the Protocol field in Tunnel Information. The following transport layer protocols are specified. Other values are reserved for future use.
When converting from an IPv6 packet, the protocol value 0x3a (ICMPv6) is changed to 0x01 (ICMP). When converting to an IPv6 packet, the protocol value 0x01 is changed to 0x3a.

The following sections describe the adjustment made to the transport layer datagram. If the datagram is fragmented, then it may be necessary to wait for multiple fragments to arrive before performing the adjustment, but the datagram MUST NOT be reassembled - each fragment must be adjusted separately.

section.name: TCP Encapsulation
section.t: The checksum field is modified as follows:

li.t: If the checksum is zero, it is not modified; otherwise, continue to step 2.
Invert all bits in the checksum.
Using one's complement arithmetic, subtract the one's complement sum of all 16 bit words in the source and destination IPv4/IPv6 addresses of the outer packet.
Invert all bits in the checksum.

section.name: TCP De-encapsulation
section.t: Perform the same adjustment as described in "TCP Encapsulation", except add the checksum of the source and destination IPv4/IPv6 addresses instead of subtracting it.

section.name: UDP Encapsulation
section.t: The checksum field is modified as follows:

li.t: If the checksum is zero, it is not modified; otherwise, continue to step 2.
If the checksum is 0xffff, then set the checksum to zero.
Invert all bits in the checksum.
Using one's complement arithmetic, subtract the one's complement sum of all 16 bit words in the source and destination IPv4/IPv6 addresses of the outer packet.
Invert all bits in the checksum.
If the checksum is zero, then set the checksum to 0xffff.

section.name: UDP De-encapsulation
section.t: Perform the same adjustment as described in "UDP Encapsulation", except add the checksum of the source and destination IPv4/IPv6 addresses instead of subtracting it.

section.name: ICMP Encapsulation
section.t: For ICMP messages which do not contain an inner packet, no adjustments are made.

For ICMP messages which do contain an inner packet, the inner packet is converted from an IPv4 packet to an IPREF UDP Tunnel Protocol packet (beginning with the Tunnel Information header). For this inner packet, the IPREF addresses are interpreted the same as in the outer packet except with the order reversed (the source IPREF address is remote, the destination IPREF address is local).
The checksum is recalculated with the new packet data if any adjustments are made.

section.name: ICMPv6 Encapsulation
section.t: The Type and Code fields are converted to their closest ICMP functional equivalents. For example, ICMPv6 Packet Too Big is converted to ICMP Fragmentation Needed.
For ICMPv6 Packet Too Big, the packet is dropped if the MTU is less than 1280; otherwise, 20 is subtracted from the MTU.

For ICMPv6 messages which contain an inner packet, the inner packet is converted from an IPv6 packet to an IPREF UDP Tunnel Protocol packet (beginning with the Tunnel Information header). For this inner packet, the IPREF addresses are interpreted the same as in the outer packet except with the order reversed (the source IPREF address is remote, the destination IPREF address is local).
The checksum is recalculated over the Type, Code, and message body. (No pseudo-header is included in the checksum calculation.)

Note that, in the case of a fragmented ICMPv6 datagram without an inner packet, it is possible to encapsulate the packet by only adjusting the first fragment in the datagram and without recalculating the checksum over the entire datagram (by using a checksum adjustment), but it is necessary to wait for the last fragment in the datagram to determine the total datagram size so that it may be subtracted from the checksum.

section.name: ICMP De-encapsulation (IPv4 Outer Header)
section.t: Perform the same adjustment as described in "ICMP Encapsulation", except converting inner packets from an IPREF UDP Tunnel Protocol packet to an IPv4 packet.

section.name: ICMPv6 De-encapsulation (IPv6 Outer Header)
section.t: The Type and Code fields are converted from ICMP to their closest ICMPv6 functional equivalents. For example, ICMP Fragmentation Needed is converted to ICMPv6 Packet Too Big.
For ICMPv6 Packet Too Big, 20 is added to the MTU.
For ICMPv6 messages which contain an inner packet, the inner packet is converted from an IPREF UDP Tunnel Protocol packet to an IPv6 packet.
The checksum is recalculated over the datagram and pseudo-header as required by ICMPv6.

As with ICMPv6 encapsulation, in the case of a fragmented ICMPv6 datagram without an inner packet, it is possible to de-encapsulate the packet by only adjusting the first fragment and waiting for the last fragment to determine the datagram length.

section.name: IPREF Reference
section.t: A reference is a 16 octet item. The most significant octet is reserved for future use. It could be flags or indicators for special purpose. They are currently not defined and should be set to zero. The rest of the reference comprises its value interpreted as an unsigned integer. The range of the values is 15 octets or 120 bits.
The reference values 0-1023 inclusive are reserved for special purpose and should not be used beyond their intended purpose. Currently, the following reserved values have been defined:

ul.li: 0 - (null reference) only consider context address when rewriting addresses
1 - reference to the gateway itself when used with ICMP messages

section.name: Reference Compression
section.t: Given the large range for reference values, many of these values may include zeros in their top bits. This creates an opportunity to compress the reference by omitting these zero bits. A reference may be viewed as comprised of four four-octet components with the reserved octet always as the most significant one.
If the particular reference value fits within a smaller range, then the reference may be compressed as shown below. The reserved octet always occupies the top position.
section.sourcecode:
┌─┬─┬─┬─┐ reference length: 4 octets │R D │ effective range: 24 bits └─┴─┴─┴─┘ A, B, C: all zeros
┌─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┐ reference length: 8 octets │R C │ D │ effective range: 56 bits └─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┘ A, B: all zeros
┌─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┐ reference length: 16 octets │R A │ B │ C │ D │ effective range: 120 bits └─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┘ A, B: not all zeros

section.name: IPREF Gateway Operation
section.t: Packets with a destination reference of 1 are addressed to the IPREF gateway itself. Gateways MUST respond with ICMP Echo Response with source reference 1 to unfragmented ICMP Echo Request addressed to this reference unless prohibited by a rate-limiting threshold or other security policy. Use of ICMP Echo Request addressed to reference 1 enables the implementation of Datagram Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (DPLPMTUD), as described by RFC 9869.

Use of other transport layer protocols from/to reference 1 is reserved for future use - gateways MUST respond with encapsulated ICMP Port Unreachable or ICMP Protocol Unreachable with source reference 1 unless prohibited by a rate-limiting threshold or other security policy.
An IPREF gateway MAY generate other encapsulated ICMP messages (eg. ICMP Echo Request, ICMP Network Unreachable, ICMP Fragmentation Needed) sent from reference 1.

section.name: IPREF Introspection Protocol
section.t: The IPREF Introspection Protocol (IIP) supports IPREF-aware implementations of troubleshooting utilities such as ping and traceroute by enabling hosts on the local network to discover IPREF addresses of themselves and remote hosts connecting over the gateway.
Implementation of IIP is OPTIONAL. IIP operates only on the local network behind an IPREF gateway; IIP packets are never sent over the tunnel.
An IIP packet has the same structure and interpretation as an IPREF UDP Tunnel Protocol packet, except:

ul.li: The UDP source and destination ports are both 1046.
The Unspecified Context (in both the source and destination fields) is interpreted as referring to the local gateway (the gateway that generated the IIP packet).

section.t: When a gateway de-encapsulates an ICMP or ICMPv6 packet, it MAY send an IIP packet at the same time, with the same source and destination addresses in the outer IPv4/IPv6 header as the ICMP/ICMPv6 packet. The IIP packet is generated by encapsulating the ICMP/ICMPv6 packet. The IIP packet may be derived from the original tunnel packet that the ICMP/ICMPv6 datagram was de-encaspulated from; however, due to the different interpretation of the Unspecified Context, it may be necessary to insert or modify the context fields. Unless both the source and destination contexts are the local IPREF gateway itself, an IIP packet must include the context fields (CP=1).
If IIP is enabled, the gateway MUST drop on encapsulation any ICMP or ICMPv6 message whose inner packet is an IIP packet.

A host on the local network can discover its own IPREF address and the IPREF address of a remote host (connecting over the IPREF gateway) by sending an ICMP Echo Request to the remote host. If IIP is enabled on the local gateway, the host should receive both an ICMP Echo Response and an IIP-encapsulated ICMP Echo Response; the IIP-encapsulated packet contains the IPREF addresses. By gradually incrementing the TTL, an IPREF-aware traceroute can be performed. Note that this does not require IIP to be enabled on the remote IPREF gateway, as IIP is a local-only protocol.

section.t: This memo includes no requests to IANA.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This document should not affect the security of the Internet. Documents describing particular pieces of IPREF might. Proper security consideration statements would be included in those documents.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.
